h1: Export plans for an Indian single malt
title: Export Plans for an Indian Single Malt | Craft Beer School
desc: How to plan exports for an Indian single malt: age rules abroad, label approval, bottle sizes, in-bond paperwork and picking a first market.
teaser: Indian single malts win respect abroad. The paperwork and the age rules decide whether your bottle can travel.
standfirst: Exporting an Indian single malt is mostly about matching your whisky to someone else's rules. Age, strength, bottle size and label wording all change at the border, so plan them before the spirit goes into the cask.
sections: Hot climate ageing meets cold climate rules

Indian heat matures whisky quickly. A malt can taste rounded in well under three years. That is a strength in the glass and a problem at customs, because many large markets define whisky by time, not taste.

The European Union and the United Kingdom both require whisky to mature for at least three years in wooden casks and to be bottled at a minimum of 40% ABV. A brilliant two year old Indian malt cannot be sold there as whisky at all. So the export plan starts in the warehouse: set aside casks that will reach three years before the market you want opens. Keep fill dates and cask numbers clean, because an importer or a regulator may ask you to prove the age of the youngest whisky in the bottle. Hot climate ageing also means more evaporation each year, so a three year old export cask holds noticeably less spirit than the same cask would in Scotland. Count that loss into the export volume. Our guide to Indian single malt explains what the category means at home.
Pick one market and learn it properly

New exporters often chase five countries at once and finish none. Pick one market, learn its rules and find one importer who already sells premium spirits there. The questions to answer for that market:

  • What is the legal definition of whisky, including minimum age and strength?
  • Which bottle sizes are allowed? The EU and UK use 70 cl. The United States long required 750 ml and has since allowed 700 ml as well; check the current rule.
  • Does the label need approval before shipping? In the US the importer files a label approval with the federal regulator before the product can be sold.
  • Which allergen, recycling, health warning or importer details must appear on the back label?
  • Who pays duty and when: the importer on arrival or a bonded warehouse later?
Your label has to be true in every language

Words that are fine in India can be a problem abroad. "Single malt" generally means malted barley only, distilled in pot stills at one distillery; many markets expect that meaning even where the law is loose. An age statement must state the age of the youngest whisky in the bottle. "Scotch" is off limits and so are names, pictures or tartans that suggest Scotland. The Scotch whisky trade body actively challenges labels that do.

Plan one master label with a removable back label per market. It is cheaper than designing a new pack every time. It also keeps the front of the bottle consistent for buyers who see it in several countries. Our guide to whisky export documentation lists the papers that travel with the goods.

Export stock usually leaves in bond, without Indian state excise duty, under a permit from the state excise department and with customs clearance at the port. The exact steps, fees and timelines vary by state and change, so work with a licensing adviser and a freight forwarder who has moved spirits before.

Plan the cash. From bottling to the importer paying you can easily take three to four months: production, permits, a few weeks at sea, clearance and the importer's own payment terms. Even a first pallet of a few hundred bottles is stock you fund for a full season before any money comes back.
Price for the shelf, then work backwards

Start with the price a buyer pays in a shop in that market, then strip out retail margin, distributor margin, importer margin, local duty and sales tax, freight and insurance. What is left is your ex-cellar price. Do this on a spreadsheet for one bottle before you talk to anyone.

Many founders do it the other way: cost plus a margin, then hope. Their bottle lands at double the price of well known single malts of the same age. The shelf price, not your cost, decides whether the importer reorders. This is exactly where knowing production cost per LPA from your own records pays off: you can see what a price really leaves you.
Build the export stock line now

Your first step: open your cask list and filter for casks that will reach three years in the next 12 to 18 months. Total their LPA and work out how many bottles at 46% that becomes. That number, not your ambition, tells you how big your first export market can be. If it is a few thousand bottles, start with one market and one importer. If it is tens of thousands, you can afford a second market a year later. Either way, the casks you fill this month decide what you can ship three years from now, so mark some of them for export on the day they are filled. Then shortlist two importers in that market and ask each for their current label and documentation checklist.
faqs: Can a two year old Indian single malt be sold in Europe?
Not as whisky. The EU and UK require at least three years in wooden casks and a minimum of 40% ABV for anything labelled whisky.
What bottle size should an export single malt use?
The EU and UK use 70 cl. The US now allows 700 ml as well as 750 ml, but confirm the current rule with your importer before printing.
Does an Indian whisky pay state excise on exports?
Export stock normally leaves in bond without state excise under a permit, but the process varies by state. Use a licensing adviser.
